questions.title: Why do the local encoder and decoder models ignore positional embeddings?
questions.question_body: In the 'Local Encoder' and 'Local Decoder' sections, the paper states: 'no positional embeddings are used in this cross-attention module.' However, earlier in the architecture description, it mentions using 'rotary positional embeddings (RoPE)' only in the global transformer's self-attention layers. Since the local models operate on byte sequences that are grouped into dynamic patches, doesn't the lack of explicit positional embeddings create an ambiguity for the model? How does the model distinguish between adjacent bytes (e.g., 'a' vs 'b') versus bytes separated by a large number of patches? I assume RoPE is applied here as well, but I want to confirm if there is a specific reason it was omitted from the local components or if it's implied to be part of the hash embeddings.

questions.title: How exactly does the 'Approx. Monotonic Constraint' prevent entropy drift over long context lengths?
questions.question_body: The paper mentions that in large-scale runs, they use an 'approximate monontonicity constraint' to avoid 'entropy drift from changes in context length,' often resetting the context with new lines (Section 3.4). However, looking at Equation (2) which defines the constraint as $H(x_t) - H(x_{t-1}) > \theta_r$, this seems to rely on comparing $H(x_t)$ to its immediate predecessor $H(x_{t-1})$. If entropy drift is cumulative over very long sequences, isn't looking only at one-step differences insufficient? Does 'resetting with new lines' mean re-initializing $H(x_0)$ for a new patch group every time a newline is encountered, effectively breaking the dependency on distant history for the threshold calculation? I am struggling to visualize how this specific mathematical condition suffices to maintain uniform information density across arbitrary document boundaries.

questions.title: In the FLOPS estimation formula for Cross Attention, what does '$r$' represent physically?
questions.question_body: In Section 3.5 ('FLOPS Estimation'), Equation (4) explicitly defines '$r$' as 'the ratio of queries to key/values' alongside '$k$, which is defined as 'the ratio of patch-dimension to byte-dimension'. In standard multi-head attention implementations where queries, keys, and values have equal dimensions and counts after projection, one would expect $r=1$. However, in BLT's cross-attention (described in Section 2.2), fixes are mentioned about maintaining multiple heads when patch representations ($h_{\mathcal{G}}$) are larger than byte representations ($h_{\mathcal{E}}$). Is '$r$' a variable that scales based on whether we are in the encoder or decoder context specifically because of this dimension mismatch? If I set up a BLT model where $h_{\mathcal{G}} = 4096$ and $h_{\mathcal{E}} = 512$, how would I calculate '$r$' explicitly in that specific scenario? Does this factor account for the overhead of concatenating heads later?

questions.title: 'Patches Scale Better Than Tokens': Why does increasing patch size reduce efficiency despite decreasing parameters per byte?
questions.question_body: The abstract claims that BLT improves efficiency by dynamically selecting long patches where data is predictable. The paper explains that larger patches mean fewer steps for the expensive Global Latent Transformer. However, I am confused about the trade-off described in Section 4 regarding Local Models. The text notes: 'When growing total parameters 20x from 400M to 8B, we only roughly double BLT's local model parameters.' This implies that as we scale up to handle more complex data (which intuitively requires smaller patches or denser global models), we aren't scaling local complexity proportionally. To what extent does increasing patch size degrade performance if we *don't* increase global model size simultaneously? Is there an upper bound on patch size beyond which even a massive Global Transformer cannot model byte-level nuances within that single step of computation?
